# Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP — Adoption Playbook

> A documentation-first knowledge base for migrating to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and for the
> design, build, and operations work that follows. Content is organized on two axes: a lifecycle
> axis (assess → design → migrate → build → operate → optimize) and a topic axis (data protection,
> data utilization, security and governance, performance, cost, multiprotocol identity).
> Findings from field technical-support work are included as anonymized reference material.

## How to read this repository

Every knowledge file under a `notes/` directory carries YAML frontmatter with an `evidence` field.
Treat it as the confidence signal:

- `verified` — reproduced by the author in the environment stated inline; `verified_on` gives the date.
- `documented` — stated in vendor or AWS documentation; `source` gives the URL.
- `field-observation` — observed once, not reproduced. Not a general rule.
- `hypothesis` — reasoned expectation, untested.

Do not present `field-observation` or `hypothesis` content as established fact. Numbers are only
meaningful together with the ONTAP version, region, and configuration stated next to them.
Naming convention used throughout: "Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP" on first mention, "FSx for ONTAP"
thereafter.

## Entry points

- [README (Japanese)](README.md): Primary hub with the two-axis navigation.
- [README (English)](docs/en/README.md): English hub, same structure.
- [Navigation guide](docs/en/navigation.md): How to pick an entry point for your question.
- [Evidence policy](docs/en/evidence-policy.md): Definition of the four evidence tiers and what each requires.
- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): Conventions, prohibitions, and verification steps for coding agents.
- [docs/agent/localization.md](docs/agent/localization.md): Path model, tiers, and switcher generation for the 8-language tree.
- [docs/agent/architecture-diagrams.md](docs/agent/architecture-diagrams.md): Icon generation, sizes, labels, and export rules for diagrams.
- [docs/agent/pitfalls.md](docs/agent/pitfalls.md): Failure modes each quality gate catches, and the fix for each.
- [docs/agent/domain-knowledge.md](docs/agent/domain-knowledge.md): Established FSx for ONTAP findings carried over from sibling repositories.

## Languages and paths

A document's language is its directory: `docs/<lang>/…` for ja, en, ko, zh-CN, zh-TW, fr, de, es.
The one exception is the Japanese hub, which is the repository-root `README.md`, so `docs/ja/README.md`
does not exist. Japanese is the reference language and the only complete tree; English covers the hub,
the guides, and every module README. The links below point at English where it exists.

Content that exists in one language only is linked in that language rather than stubbed out, so a
missing translation is an absent link, never a placeholder page.

## Lifecycle playbooks

- [01 Assess](docs/en/playbooks/01-assess/): Inventory of the current NAS and identification of migration constraints.
- [02 Design](docs/en/playbooks/02-design/): Capacity, throughput, protocol, and protection scheme selection.
- [03 Migrate](docs/en/playbooks/03-migrate/): Method selection, cutover sequencing, and rollback.
- [04 Build](docs/en/playbooks/04-build/): Infrastructure as code, automation, reproducible builds.
- [05 Operate](docs/en/playbooks/05-operate/): Monitoring, capacity management, incident response, change management.
- [06 Optimize](docs/en/playbooks/06-optimize/): Performance and cost tuning after steady state.

## Topic domains

- [Data protection](docs/en/domains/data-protection/): Snapshot, SnapMirror, SnapLock, backup and ransomware readiness.
- [Data utilization](docs/en/domains/data-utilization/): Analytics, AI and RAG, access over the S3 API.
- [Security and governance](docs/en/domains/security-governance/): Encryption, audit, permission design, regulated workload considerations.
- [Performance](docs/en/domains/performance/): Throughput design, latency, caching, shared bandwidth behavior.
- [Cost](docs/en/domains/cost/): Capacity, tiering, and the gap between estimates and measurements.
- [Multiprotocol identity](docs/en/domains/multiprotocol-identity/): NFS and SMB coexistence, Active Directory integration, ID mapping.
- [Block storage](docs/en/domains/block-storage/): iSCSI and NVMe/TCP, LUN layout, multipathing, and how capacity is counted.

## Findings available today

- [AWS Transform's Finalize is where physical capacity peaks](docs/ja/playbooks/03-migrate/notes/atx-finalize-flexclone-capacity.md): The MGN SNAPSHOT phase is an ONTAP volume Snapshot and LAUNCH is a FlexClone from it, so the target volume holds 35.5 MiB of physical space against 7.91 GiB logical until Finalize. Finalize splits that clone, taking it to 8.57 GiB while the staging volume is still present for about nine minutes, so one extra full copy of the migrated data has to be free. Planning aggregate capacity from the pre-Finalize figure under-provisions. Measured once on 8 GiB in ap-northeast-1 on ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1.
All twelve modules have content. Each module README lists the questions it covers alongside the note
that answers each one; a question whose answer is not yet written is marked `_未追加_`, so the module
READMEs are the authoritative source for coverage rather than any count stated here.
Each file below is one concern, carries its primary sources, and ends with a procedure for checking the
claim in your own environment. All are Japanese; the English module READMEs link to each one.

- [Free space does not mean you can still write](docs/ja/playbooks/01-assess/notes/counting-bytes-is-not-counting-files.md): An inventory has to count files, not only bytes. The default inode count stops growing past 648 GiB, so a large volume holding small files exhausts inodes long before capacity and then rejects writes.
- [ACL preservation is a privilege problem, not a tool problem](docs/ja/playbooks/03-migrate/notes/preserving-acls-during-migration.md): Defaults omit ACLs, and an account lacking the right privilege skips unreadable ones silently while still exiting successfully. "No errors" is not evidence of preservation.
- [Monitoring fails on averages](docs/ja/playbooks/05-operate/notes/monitoring-fails-on-averages.md): The statistic has to be chosen before the threshold. Standby file servers and unsaturated aggregates pull an average down, and SSD utilization changes behavior at 90% and 98%, not only at the recommended 80%.
- [Pre-production review](docs/ja/playbooks/04-build/checklists/pre-production-review.md): Checklist of the irreversible settings, and of what to exercise before going live.
- [Cutover-day checklist](docs/ja/playbooks/03-migrate/checklists/cutover.md): Ordered by when each step happens relative to the outage, because downtime is only the interval between stopping clients and resuming them — the transfer finishes before that. Separates what can be done while clients are still running, names the four SnapMirror mistakes that force a fresh baseline sync, and treats rollback as a decision about data already written rather than a configuration to revert.
- [Inventory checklist](docs/ja/playbooks/01-assess/checklists/inventory.md): Each item states which later, irreversible decision it feeds, and anything without such a use is deliberately excluded. Covers file counts rather than bytes alone, whether the copying account can read every ACL, actual protocol use as opposed to configured protocols, and the largest file size, since above 50 GiB an S3 access point cannot be the write path.
- [The rollback window closes when clients start writing](docs/ja/playbooks/03-migrate/notes/where-the-rollback-window-closes.md): A SnapMirror destination is read-only until the relationship is broken and breaking it does not affect the source, so rollback is free until clients write to the destination. After that there is no operation that undoes a cutover. Incremental transfer depends on the newest common snapshot, so deleting SnapMirror's snapshots on the source forces a full baseline again.
- [The IaC boundary is set by the API surface](docs/ja/playbooks/04-build/notes/what-iac-cannot-reach.md): File systems, SVMs, volumes, backups and tags are template-managed, but SMB encryption enforcement, the volume inode maximum and FlexVol-to-FlexGroup conversion are ONTAP CLI only, so a successful template is not a complete configuration. Omitting SvmAdminPassword forces the use of fsxadmin and costs least privilege.
- [Maintenance cannot be deferred past 14 days](docs/ja/playbooks/05-operate/notes/maintenance-cannot-be-deferred.md): ONTAP patching is performed by the service and a maintenance window must occur at least once every 14 days, after which maintenance proceeds regardless. SSD above 90% causes throughput to be throttled during patching, and on Multi-AZ a missing route with no room in the route table disconnects clients for the duration.
- [Enabling SnapLock is not the same as locking](docs/ja/domains/data-protection/notes/snaplock-and-layered-ransomware-readiness.md): Three separate irreversible decisions - enabling SnapLock, the retention mode, and permanently disabling privileged delete. Privileged delete is Enterprise only, needs an audit log volume in the same SVM first, and cannot be used once retention has expired.
- [An S3 access point authorizes every request as one identity](docs/ja/domains/data-utilization/notes/reaching-data-without-copies.md): FileSystemIdentity authorizes all file access requests made through the access point, so the original per-file ACLs do not carry into an analytics or RAG pipeline reading through it. Retrieval scoping has to be designed in the index. Also covers when FlexCache helps: read-heavy workloads with infrequent changes.
- [p99 cannot be read from the CloudWatch metrics](docs/ja/domains/performance/notes/what-you-cannot-read-from-cloudwatch.md): The volume latency metrics expose total time and total operation count with Sum as the valid statistic, so dividing them yields an average and tail latency has to be measured at the client. Benchmarks are also swayed by burst credit balance, so a run that does not record the balance does not reproduce.
- [The AD dependency lasts the lifetime, not just the join](docs/ja/domains/multiprotocol-identity/notes/ad-dependency-lasts-the-lifetime.md): A valid service account is required for the lifetime of the file system because replacing a failed file system or SVM and patching ONTAP both require unjoining and rejoining the domain. An expired credential is symptomless until then, and patching cannot be deferred past 14 days.
- [Deployment type is decided once](docs/ja/playbooks/02-design/notes/deployment-type-is-decided-once.md): Deployment type cannot be changed after creation, and the same choice fixes the scale-out ceiling. Only second-generation Single-AZ supports more than one HA pair, so "start Multi-AZ and add pairs later" is not available. Added HA pairs cannot be removed, and past six pairs iSCSI and NVMe/TCP stop being available.
- [Tiering defaults differ by creation method](docs/ja/playbooks/06-optimize/notes/tiering-defaults-differ-by-creation-method.md): The console defaults a volume to Auto with a 31-day cooling period while the CLI, API and ONTAP CLI default to Snapshot Only with 2 days, so a console-built test environment and an IaC-built production one tier differently. Whether a read promotes data back to SSD also depends on the policy and on whether the read is random or sequential.
- [At rest is automatic, in transit is off by default](docs/ja/domains/security-governance/notes/what-the-platform-gives-and-what-stays-yours.md): Encryption at rest cannot be disabled, while encryption in transit is not enabled by default and Kerberos for NFS and SMB requires the SVM to be joined to Active Directory or LDAP. SMB access auditing records only the first read and first write per object, so read counts cannot be answered from it.
- [Billing splits into provisioned and consumed](docs/ja/domains/cost/notes/provisioned-versus-consumed.md): SSD capacity, SSD IOPS and throughput are billed on what is provisioned; capacity pool and backups on what is consumed. Capacity pool also carries per-read and per-write request charges, so tiering data that turns out to be read regularly can cost more. Deduplication and compression do not lower the bill unless provisioned capacity is reduced.
- [Having snapshots is not the same as being able to recover](docs/ja/domains/data-protection/notes/snapshots-are-not-a-recovery-plan.md): Snapshot, backup and SnapMirror cover different failure domains. A snapshot lives inside the same file system and is lost with it, and only read-write volumes can be backed up.
- [A backup copy needs no file system until you restore](docs/ja/domains/data-protection/notes/backup-copies-across-regions-and-accounts.md): Backups can be copied to another Region and, through AWS Backup with AWS Organizations, to another account, but the restore target is still confined to the Region the backup is stored in — so the destination file system and SVM are created at recovery time and that lands on RTO. Restoring always produces a new volume, there is no path back to the original one, and a volume being restored reports its type as DP until the restore completes.
- [Volume security style decides the permission model](docs/ja/domains/multiprotocol-identity/notes/security-style-and-permission-evaluation.md): Blocking ID mapping does not block SMB access on an NTFS-style volume, because that path evaluates the NTFS ACL directly.
- [Throughput is not set by one value](docs/ja/domains/performance/notes/where-throughput-is-determined-and-shared.md): Generation, configuration and Region all move the ceiling, and a FlexVol cannot exceed a single HA pair regardless of how many pairs the file system has.
- [FSx for ONTAP S3 access points are not "S3 you can use as S3"](docs/ja/domains/data-utilization/notes/s3-access-point-constraints.md): Same-account and same-Region prerequisites are plan-level constraints, and enabling access points lowers the volume-count ceiling. Two behaviours that look like limits are defects rather than intended restrictions: Unicode characters rejected in object tags, and UploadPartCopy failing within one access point. Treat those as waiting on a fix, not as constraints to design around.
- [S3 Access Point authorization design — evaluation order and the two layers that narrow access](docs/ja/domains/security-governance/notes/access-point-authorization-layers.md): A request through an FSx for ONTAP S3 access point clears two independent layers: AWS-side IAM authorization, where an explicit Deny is what narrows, and file-system permissions, where the identity bound to the access point is evaluated against mode bits or ACLs. There is no bucket policy — what you set is an access point policy — and within the same account a narrower Allow does not narrow anything, because identity-based and resource-based policies are combined. Measured on the AWS side: a policy-less access point is still usable, an action absent from the Allow list still succeeds, `Deny` with `NotPrincipal` denies the principal it was meant to exempt unless the role ARN, the assumed-role session ARN and the account ARN are all listed, `aws:SecureTransport` never reaches its Deny branch because HTTP is redirected before authorization, cross-account data access works (the same-account requirement constrains creating the access point, not using it), and `aws:PrincipalOrgID` is what stops a principal from another organization. Measured on the file-system side: changing only the volume root owner and mode bits flips PutObject between AccessDenied and success with no policy attached; neither LDAP nor an Active Directory join is required, since an SVM-local UNIX user and a workgroup-mode local Windows user both worked; ONTAP file access auditing records only the SID of the bound identity with the name unresolved and an AWS service-side SubjectIP that varies between requests, so identifying the caller requires CloudTrail; and a UNIX-style volume carrying only mode bits produced zero audit records even with auditing enabled on the SVM, while attaching an audit ACE via SLAG broke the data path. Six reusable policy examples plus the full parameter table showing that everything except the policy is fixed at creation. Available in Japanese and English.
- [Migrating from SaaS starts with classifying the source](docs/en/playbooks/03-migrate/notes/saas-source-migration-scoping.md): What to settle before choosing a transfer method — whether the source exposes a storage endpoint, whether tenant admin authorization can be issued for the migration window, and how many sharing forms have no counterpart in an NFS or SMB ACL. Also the Assess numbers the later decisions need, including the largest file size, since above 50 GiB the file cannot be written through an S3 access point. Available in Japanese and English; the transfer mechanisms are deliberately left in the linked primary source rather than restated.

- [The block protocol choice is narrowed before you make it](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/protocol-choice-is-bounded-before-you-choose.md): NVMe/TCP requires a second-generation file system and iSCSI requires six or fewer HA pairs, and neither generation nor deployment type can be changed after creation. Both protocols use the same two per-SVM LIFs and differ only by port, and port 4420 for NVMe/TCP is absent from the AWS security-group requirements table, so a group written for iSCSI fails as a timeout. There is no documented AWS procedure for NVMe/TCP on Windows.
- [LUN layout decides recovery granularity](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/lun-layout-decides-recovery-granularity.md): Snapshot and SnapMirror act on the volume, so LUNs sharing a volume get mutually consistent copies but cannot be restored individually. NetApp states that one LUN per volume is not a formal best practice, and two AWS posts recommend different layouts. `lun move` was non-disruptive on a mounted, actively written LUN and preserved the WWID. A FlexClone whose relationship record outlives the clone volume can make the parent volume, its SVM and the whole file system undeletable.
- [Capacity is counted in three places](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/capacity-is-counted-in-three-places.md): 1,024 GiB of provisioned SSD produced a 907.03 GiB aggregate on Single-AZ and 861.7 GiB on Multi-AZ, a 100 GiB volume reported 95 GiB of active file system because of the 5 percent snapshot reserve, and a 20 GiB space-reserved LUN consumed 20.078 GiB with nothing written. That accounting appears between 0 and 30 seconds after the change, so an immediate read returns the previous value. Deleting a file inside a LUN returns nothing until TRIM, and the freed blocks then move into snapshot usage if a snapshot exists.
- [Paths are the failover mechanism](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/paths-are-the-failover-mechanism.md): Following the AWS instruction of eight sessions per node against two LIFs produced 16 paths per LUN, split evenly between ALUA optimized and non-optimized, against NetApp guidance that a single LUN needs no more than four. Re-running the Windows connection loop is not idempotent and took the host from 16 to 24 paths. A measured failover, induced by a throughput-capacity change because `storage failover show` returns an empty table to fsxadmin, left iSCSI over dm-multipath with zero failures across 1,161 one-second direct writes and a single 2.101 second stall, while an NVMe/TCP namespace on the same host was unavailable for 423.8 seconds — Amazon Linux 2023 ships without CONFIG_NVME_MULTIPATH, so one namespace appears as two block devices with no path for the application to fail over to.
- [A snapshot of a LUN is crash-consistent by default](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/a-snapshot-of-a-lun-is-crash-consistent.md): The application-consistent flag exists for record keeping and, in NetApp's words, makes no difference from ONTAP's perspective; quiescing is done by something outside the storage, such as SnapCenter, which AWS states carries no additional licensing cost on FSx for ONTAP. A clone taken from a snapshot mounted with the pre-snapshot content intact after an XFS log recovery, and required `-o nouuid` when the parent was mounted on the same host because it carries the original's filesystem UUID. A database spanning separate volumes is recoverable from a crash-consistent snapshot when a consistency group applies a write fence, correcting an earlier claim in this note that it was not.
- [LUNs and igroups sit outside the AWS API](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/block-objects-are-outside-the-aws-api.md): CloudFormation exposes six Amazon FSx resource types and the Amazon FSx API has no block action, so provisioning crosses from the AWS control plane to ONTAP between the volume and the LUN. The volume is the one object reachable from both, and the choice matters: a volume created on the ONTAP side receives no fsvol identifier and is therefore absent from CloudWatch, from AWS API tagging and from AWS Backup, so creating the volume through the AWS API and only the LUN through ONTAP is what keeps the two halves aligned. The NetApp Terraform provider covers LUN, igroup, LUN map, iSCSI service and NVMe namespace but has no NVMe subsystem resource, so NVMe/TCP cannot be completed in Terraform alone; the Ansible collection does cover it.
- [When shared block changes the design](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/when-shared-block-changes-the-design.md): Amazon EBS is the straightforward choice for a single attachment, and an FSx for ONTAP LUN cannot be a boot volume. What changes the design is file and block from one file system, snapshots consuming provisioned capacity rather than a separate charge, SnapMirror operating on a volume containing LUNs, and FlexClone without a data copy. The million-IOPS figure widely cited is ten file systems combined under LVM in 2022, when one file system was capped at 80,000 IOPS.
- [Kubernetes block volumes meet the volume limit](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/kubernetes-block-volumes-and-the-volume-limit.md): Trident's ontap-san driver creates one FlexVol plus one LUN per persistent volume, so the persistent volume count runs into the volume limit of 500 per HA pair or 1,000 in total rather than into capacity. ontap-san-economy packs many LUNs into shared FlexVols to lift that ceiling, at the cost of no longer being able to apply volume-level snapshots, SnapMirror or QoS per persistent volume.
- [Multi-AZ moves a route, not an address](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/multi-az-moves-a-route-not-an-address.md): On a Multi-AZ file system the NFS, SMB and management addresses sit outside the VPC CIDR and fail over by rewriting the target ENI of a /32 entry in the associated route table, while the iSCSI and NVMe/TCP addresses are ordinary in-VPC addresses with failover-policy disabled that never move — so block access needs no Transit Gateway across a peering, and its availability is entirely host-side multipath. The ALUA and ANA optimized path follows the node that owns the volume, not the client's Availability Zone, so a client in the standby AZ sends its optimized traffic across the AZ boundary.
- [igroups are not the only access control](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/igroups-are-not-the-only-access-control.md): CHAP and portsets both work as fsxadmin and neither appears in the AWS documentation. iSCSI authentication defaults to none, so an igroup alone admits anyone who can name a listed IQN; a login without credentials exits 24 with "Initiator failed authentication with target". A portset genuinely reduces the path count but leaves the excluded path on the host as a faulty, zero-byte device that must be deleted through sysfs. `storage failover show` returns an empty table rather than an authorization error, so there is no takeover command to induce a failover with.
- [A database on LUNs recovers without quiescing](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/a-database-on-luns-recovers-without-quiescing.md): A PostgreSQL instance with its data directory and WAL on separate LUNs was captured mid-write by a consistency-group snapshot with a write fence, which returned in 0.52 seconds and produced an identical create-time on both volumes. Clones mapped to another host's igroup started with no preparation, replayed WAL in 0.84 seconds and retained every row committed before the fence. `pg_backup_start` was never used, and `-o nouuid` was unnecessary because the parent was not mounted on the same host.
- [What block monitoring shows](docs/ja/domains/block-storage/notes/what-block-monitoring-shows.md): The `AWS/FSx` namespace has no LUN dimension and no protocol dimension, so iSCSI, NVMe/TCP and NFS traffic are indistinguishable in CloudWatch. Volume-scope I/O metrics do exist, which makes one LUN per volume a monitoring decision as well as a recovery-granularity one, and the FileServer dimension carries node names and is where a failover becomes visible. A volume created on the ONTAP side receives no fsvol identifier, so it is absent from CloudWatch, from AWS API tagging and from AWS Backup.
## Reference

Written as bilingual single files: Japanese and English prose share the same tables, so these links
serve both languages and there is no separate `docs/en/reference/` tree.

- [Decision trees](docs/ja/reference/decision-trees/): Selection and evaluation flowcharts. [Choosing a migration method](docs/ja/reference/decision-trees/migration-method.md) branches on whether the source is ONTAP, on SnapMirror version compatibility, and on ACL preservation requirements. [How a request through an S3 access point is decided](docs/ja/reference/decision-trees/access-point-authorization.md) follows the two-layer authorization order — implicit deny, then any explicit Deny, then Organizations RCPs and SCPs, then identity-based and resource-based policies as a union within an account but as a conjunction across accounts, and finally the single file system identity the access point is bound to — and includes a table that works back from a symptom, such as an AccessDenied while IAM allows the call, to the layer that refused.
- [Comparison matrices](docs/ja/reference/comparison/): Option comparisons with trade-offs stated symmetrically for every option. Two are available: [data protection methods](docs/ja/reference/comparison/data-protection-methods.md) covering snapshot, volume backup, AWS Backup and SnapMirror plus the two SnapLock modes, and [tiering policies](docs/ja/reference/comparison/tiering-policies.md) covering NONE, SNAPSHOT_ONLY, AUTO and ALL.
- [Limits and quotas](docs/ja/reference/limits/): Limit values with source and verification date.
- [Glossary](docs/ja/reference/glossary/): ONTAP and AWS terminology.
- [Block storage resource map](docs/ja/reference/block-storage-resource-map.md): Index of the AWS, NetApp, re:Post and public infrastructure-as-code sources for block storage, plus a table of the seven places those sources disagree with each other.

## Workshop delivery

Japanese-only. Knowledge about running a public AWS Workshop Studio workshop inside a community
event's time budget, not a restatement of the workshop's own instructions.

- [Workshop Studio delivery notes](docs/ja/workshop-studio/): What a published workshop does not tell you — measured durations, which modules to drop, and the dependencies between them.
- [Fitting the EDA zero-copy scenario into 90 minutes](docs/ja/workshop-studio/eda-s3-access-points-90min/): Module selection and a timetable for the FSx for ONTAP S3 access point workshop. Machine time across the selected modules totals about 35 seconds, so the only hard constraint is the Amazon Quick knowledge base sync, which has to be started early and overlapped with another module.
- [Measured timings](docs/ja/workshop-studio/eda-s3-access-points-90min/measured-timings.md): Log generation takes 2.5 seconds against a stated 90 seconds; access point creation reaches AVAILABLE in 14 seconds; five Athena queries run in 2-3 seconds each. Environment stated alongside every number, and the unmeasured modules are listed as unmeasured.
- [Where a self-hosted run breaks](docs/ja/workshop-studio/eda-s3-access-points-90min/facilitation-risks.md): Three failures whose error messages point away from the cause — a Glue crawler blocked by Lake Formation, region hardcoded into policy ARNs surfacing as access denied, and IAM propagation making the first attempt fail.

## Case studies

- [Case studies](docs/en/case-studies/): Three kinds are kept apart so a reader can tell whose environment is being described. Public case studies published by AWS or NetApp are organized as a linked index; field cases are generalized lessons from technical-support work; verification cases are observations in this repository's own environment. Field and verification cases contain no company names, no real identifiers, and no configurations that could identify an organization.
- [Published case studies by industry and workload](docs/ja/case-studies/public-case-studies.md): A linked index of AWS and NetApp case studies, searchable along two axes — industry (energy, semiconductor/EDA, financial services, healthcare, medical devices, telecom, public health and education, media, IT) and workload (NAS migration, SQL Server, EDA, SaaS tenancy, hybrid and branch caching, media production, multi-Region). Figures from those accounts are deliberately not restated: most published case studies omit the ONTAP version, Region, configuration and measurement method, so they establish where a topic is discussed rather than a value to design against.
